newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese stocks manage mild recovery in edgy trade.
newsitem.headline: Japanese stocks manage mild recovery in edgy trade.

text.p: Japanese stocks made a mild recovery on Monday after last week's precipitous drop, but few players thought the worst was over for the slumping share market.

The market got off to an edgy start, with the key Nikkei average dropping close to the key 17,000 level in morning trade, but investors backed off and buying kicked in to push the benchmark back into positive territory by mid-session.
But analysts called the rebound feeble and largely technical, saying the market remained gripped by worries about the economy and the health of some financial institutions.
"We are not sure whether the selling has reached a climax," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager at Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
The 225-share Nikkei average, the market's main barometer, ended the morning session up a marginal 41.23 points or 0.24 percent at 17,344.88 after earlier dipping as low as 17,019.56.
The Nikkei lost more than 2,000 points last week alone due to spreading gloom over the government's ability to keep the nation's economic recovery on track.

The Topix index -- a broader measure of the market than the blue-chip dominated Nikkei -- closed the morning with a loss, falling 0.91 point or 0.07 percent to 1,336.12, underlining the frailty of the recovery.

The sustained flight from stocks has fuelled fears of a major meltdown on Japanese markets as investors, already deterred by low Japanese interest rates, look elsewhere for reliable returns on their money.
Brokers said the stock market was still vulnerable, despite signs that the Nikkei had found a floor at 17,000 points.
Investors bought up banking and brokerage shares in early trade after last week's fall left them ripe for bargain-hunting, but the interest later waned.

Bank shares have been hit by worries that the slumping stock market may erode unrealised profits on share portfolios which the banks have been using in the fight against heaps of bad loans left from the 1980s "bubble" era.
Shares in Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd were buoyed initially but slipped back under renewed worries about the bad loan problem, shedding 90 yen to stand at 1,900 yen by midday.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, another major bank, also came under selling pressure, falling 26 yen to 238 yen.
The market mood remained pessimistic, with brokers and investors still licking the wounds left by last week's dive, which was driven by weakness in the financial sector.
On Friday alone, the Nikkei tumbled 770.22 points or 4.26 percent to close at 17,303.65, the largest single-day drop since January 23, 1995.

"Unless the market can find common ground with the government over their views of the economy, the stocks' downward trend will not change," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
Analysts said that only really solid floor for the Nikkei on charts is seen at the 14,000 level.
The U.S. dollar, meanwhile, hovered near 116 yen in morning Tokyo on Monday but remained directionless, after closing in New York at around 116.10 yen on Friday.

Further stock tumbles could encourage yen selling. But some players regard the weakness as a supportive factor for the yen as a further decline in shares would prompt investors to liquidate foreign assets to offset losses on domestic stocks.
Japanese government bond (JGB) futures rose in Tokyo morning trade. The key March futures ended the morning session up 0.44 at 125.81 after rising as high as 125.88.
